claim: The preBötzinger complex (preBötC) is a region that is both necessary and sufficient for inspiration.
source: A region that is both necessary and sufficient for inspiration, the pre-Bötzinger Complex (preBötC), is autorhythmic and forms the core of this network (Smith et al., 1991; Tan et al., 2008; Vann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 1991; Tan et al., 2008; Vann et al., 2018

claim: The preBötC is autorhythmic and forms the core of the inspiratory network.
source: A region that is both necessary and sufficient for inspiration, the pre-Bötzinger Complex (preBötC), is autorhythmic and forms the core of this network (Smith et al., 1991; Tan et al., 2008; Vann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 1991; Tan et al., 2008; Vann et al., 2018

claim: The frequency of breathing changes during sleep/wake states, exercise, environmental challenges, and orofacial behaviors such as feeding and vocalization.
source: Like many rhythmic networks, a critical characteristic of the preBötC is that the frequency of its output is dynamic - the rate of breathing changes during for example sleep/wake states, exercise, environmental challenges, and orofacial behaviors such as feeding and vocalization (Moore et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moore et al., 2013; Ramirez et al., 2016

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory inputs from other brain regions, as well as neuromodulation, can potently facilitate or depress the frequency of breathing.
source: Excitatory and inhibitory inputs from other brain regions, as well as neuromodulation, can potently facilitate or depress the frequency of breathing (Doi and Ramirez, 2008; Zuperku et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doi and Ramirez, 2008; Zuperku et al., 2017

claim: Glutamatergic synaptic interactions among preBötC interneurons are obligatory for rhythmogenesis.
source: Glutamatergic synaptic interactions among preBötC interneurons allow this sparsely connected network (Carroll and Ramirez, 2013; Schwab et al., 2010) to periodically synchronize and are therefore obligatory for rhythmogenesis (Ge and Feldman, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ge and Feldman, 1998

claim: The preBötC is a sparsely connected network.
source: Glutamatergic synaptic interactions among preBötC interneurons allow this sparsely connected network (Carroll and Ramirez, 2013; Schwab et al., 2010) to periodically synchronize and are therefore obligatory for rhythmogenesis (Ge and Feldman, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carroll and Ramirez, 2013; Schwab et al., 2010

claim: Unrestrained feed-forward excitation in the preBötC network leads to hyper synchronization during inspiratory bursts, which subsequently causes a prolonged period of reduced network excitability.
source: However, if left unrestrained, feed-forward excitation in the network leads to hyper synchronization during inspiratory bursts, which subsequently causes a prolonged period of reduced network excitability (Baertsch et al., 2018; Kottick and Del Negro, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baertsch et al., 2018; Kottick and Del Negro, 2015

claim: Inhibitory interactions within the preBötC are critical for limiting synchronization during bursts.
source: Inhibitory interactions within the preBötC are critical for limiting synchronization during bursts (Harris et al., 2017) and reducing the subsequent refractoriness of the network (Baertsch et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2017; Baertsch et al., 2018

claim: Inhibitory interactions within the preBötC reduce the subsequent refractoriness of the network.
source: Inhibitory interactions within the preBötC are critical for limiting synchronization during bursts (Harris et al., 2017) and reducing the subsequent refractoriness of the network (Baertsch et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baertsch et al., 2018

claim: Roughly 40% of inspiratory preBötC neurons are inhibitory (GABAergic and/or glycinergic).
source: Indeed, roughly 40% of inspiratory preBötC neurons are inhibitory (GABAergic and/or glycinergic) (Oke et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2009; Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) and by regulating the excitability of glutamatergic neurons during inspiratory bursts, these neurons play an important role in controlling breathing frequency.
evidence: Supported by citations to Oke et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2009; Morgado-Valle et al., 2010

claim: Inhibitory neurons in the preBötC play an important role in controlling breathing frequency by regulating the excitability of glutamatergic neurons during inspiratory bursts.
source: Indeed, roughly 40% of inspiratory preBötC neurons are inhibitory (GABAergic and/or glycinergic) (Oke et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2009; Morgado-Valle et al., 2010) and by regulating the excitability of glutamatergic neurons during inspiratory bursts, these neurons play an important role in controlling breathing frequency.
evidence: Supported by citations to Oke et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2009; Morgado-Valle et al., 2010

claim: Recurrent excitatory synaptic connections and ectopic bursting of individual preBötC neurons give rise to a gradual increase in network excitability that drives the onset of the next burst during the inter-burst interval.
source: During the time between bursts, referred to as the inter-burst interval (IBI), recurrent excitatory synaptic connections (Del Negro et al., 2018) and ectopic bursting of individual preBötC neurons (Ramirez et al., 2004) are thought to give rise to a gradual increase in network excitability that drives the onset of the next burst.
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Negro et al., 2018; Ramirez et al., 2004

claim: Spontaneous spiking activity in a small subset of excitatory preBötC neurons begins to percolate stochastically through the network during the inter-burst interval, gradually recruiting more spiking activity among interconnected excitatory neurons.
source: In this model, spontaneous spiking activity in a small subset of excitatory preBötC neurons begins to percolate stochastically through the network, gradually recruiting more spiking activity among interconnected excitatory neurons (Kam et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kam et al., 2013b

claim: During the percolation phase, activation of membrane voltage- and calcium-dependent conductances in an increasing number of neurons causes the excitation to become exponential, culminating in an inspiratory burst.
source: During this percolation phase, activation of membrane voltage- and calcium-dependent conductances in an increasing number of neurons causes the excitation to become exponential, culminating in an inspiratory burst (Del Negro et al., 2010; Ramirez et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Negro et al., 2010; Ramirez et al., 2016

claim: The gradual increase in spiking activity during the percolation phase, or 'pre-inspiratory ramp', is thought to be primarily mediated by a subset of glutamatergic preBötC interneurons that have enhanced excitability.
source: The gradual increase in spiking activity during this phase, or 'pre-inspiratory ramp', is thought to be primarily mediated by a subset of glutamatergic preBötC interneurons that have enhanced excitability.
evidence: Based on inference from the described model of percolation

claim: Glutamatergic preBötC interneurons with enhanced excitability are derived from V0-lineage precursors and express the transcription factor Dbx1 during development.
source: Derived from V0-lineage precursors, these neurons express the transcription factor developing brain homeobox one protein (Dbx1) during development (referred to here as 'Dbx1 neurons') (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Picardo et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017

claim: Substance P is a key mediator of many physiological and neurobiological processes.
source: A member of the tachykinin neuropeptide family, SP is a key mediator of many physiological and neurobiological processes (Mantyh, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mantyh, 2002

claim: Substance P regulates the stability of the respiratory rhythm.
source: For breathing, SP regulates the stability of the respiratory rhythm (Ben-Mabrouk and Tryba, 2010; Yeh et al., 2017) as well as respiratory responses to hypoxia (Chen et al., 1990; Ptak et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ben-Mabrouk and Tryba, 2010; Yeh et al., 2017

claim: Substance P regulates respiratory responses to hypoxia.
source: For breathing, SP regulates the stability of the respiratory rhythm (Ben-Mabrouk and Tryba, 2010; Yeh et al., 2017) as well as respiratory responses to hypoxia (Chen et al., 1990; Ptak et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 1990; Ptak et al., 2002

claim: The endogenous receptor for substance P, neurokinin one receptor (NK1R), is expressed on only ~5–7% of CNS neurons.
source: The endogenous receptor for SP, neurokinin one receptor (NK1R), is expressed on only ~5–7% of CNS neurons (Mantyh, 2002), but is enriched in the preBötC (Gray et al., 1999; Schwarzacher et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mantyh, 2002

claim: NK1R is enriched in the preBötC.
source: The endogenous receptor for SP, neurokinin one receptor (NK1R), is expressed on only ~5–7% of CNS neurons (Mantyh, 2002), but is enriched in the preBötC (Gray et al., 1999; Schwarzacher et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gray et al., 1999; Schwarzacher et al., 2011

claim: Substance P binding to NK1R causes excitation of preBötC neurons through coupling with voltage-independent cation channels.
source: SP binding to NK1R causes excitation of preBötC neurons through coupling with voltage-independent cation channels (Hayes and Del Negro, 2007; Ptak et al., 2009), including sodium leak channel, non-selective (Nalcn).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayes and Del Negro, 2007; Ptak et al., 2009

claim: Substance P binding to NK1R causes excitation of preBötC neurons through coupling with Nalcn.
source: SP binding to NK1R causes excitation of preBötC neurons through coupling with voltage-independent cation channels (Hayes and Del Negro, 2007; Ptak et al., 2009), including sodium leak channel, non-selective (Nalcn).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayes and Del Negro, 2007; Ptak et al., 2009

claim: Disruption of the Nalcn ion channel causes pathological respiratory instability.
source: Disruption of this ion channel causes pathological respiratory instability (Yeh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yeh et al., 2017

claim: Substance P promotes robust facilitation of inspiratory frequency.
source: SP also promotes robust facilitation of inspiratory frequency (Gray et al., 1999; Peña and Ramirez, 2004b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gray et al., 1999; Peña and Ramirez, 2004b

claim: In response to substance P, inspiratory burst frequency increased from 0.23 ± 0.02 Hz to 0.31 ± 0.03 Hz (p=0.003).
source: In response to SP, inspiratory burst frequency increased from 0.23 ± 0.02 Hz to 0.31 ± 0.03 Hz (p=0.003) during steady state SP (>~3 min post bath application) similar to previous observations in transverse slice preparations (Peña and Ramirez, 2004b).
evidence: Experimental data from n=6 experiments with statistical analysis

claim: The refractory period was not altered by substance P despite a frequency increase of 31.9 ± 5.6%.
source: However, despite a frequency increase of 31.9 ± 5.6%, the refractory period was not altered by SP (non-linear regression analysis; p>0.05).
evidence: Experimental data with statistical analysis (non-linear regression)

claim: In substance P, the average inter-burst interval became shorter (4.5 ± 0.4 s to 3.5 ± 0.5 s; paired t-test; p<0.0002).
source: As a result, the average IBI became shorter (4.5 ± 0.4 s to 3.5 ± 0.5 s; paired t-test; p<0.0002) and less variable (SD of 1.3 ± 0.1 to 0.84 ± 0.1; p<0.0139) in SP (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data with statistical analysis (paired t-test)

claim: In substance P, the inter-burst interval became less variable (SD of 1.3 ± 0.1 to 0.84 ± 0.1; p<0.0139).
source: As a result, the average IBI became shorter (4.5 ± 0.4 s to 3.5 ± 0.5 s; paired t-test; p<0.0002) and less variable (SD of 1.3 ± 0.1 to 0.84 ± 0.1; p<0.0139) in SP (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Substance P increases the frequency and regularity of the inspiratory rhythm through differential modulation of two inspiratory phases: The refractory phase remains unchanged, while the duration of the recurrent excitation or percolation phase is reduced.
source: Together these data suggest that SP increases the frequency and regularity of the inspiratory rhythm through differential modulation of two inspiratory phases: The refractory phase remains unchanged, while the duration of the recurrent excitation or percolation phase, which promotes the onset of the subsequent burst, is reduced.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing unchanged refractory period but shortened IBI

claim: Excitatory neurons in the preBötC can be grouped based on the presence or absence of spiking during the inter-burst interval that typically increases in frequency, or 'ramps', before the subsequent inspiratory burst.
source: However, excitatory neurons could be clearly grouped based on the presence or absence of spiking during the IBI that typically increases in frequency, or 'ramps', before the subsequent inspiratory burst – often referred to as 'pre-inspiratory (pre-I)' activity.
evidence: Experimental observation from n=29 recorded neurons

claim: No inspiratory inhibitory neurons in the preBötC were identified with pre-inspiratory spiking.
source: In contrast, we did not identify any inspiratory inhibitory neurons in the preBötC with pre-I spiking (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation from n=7 inhibitory neurons

claim: Excitatory neurons with pre-inspiratory spiking (n = 9) had inspiratory spike frequencies ranging from 12.0 to 50.8 Hz (mean: 28.0 ± 4.4 Hz) and burst durations ranging from 272 to 763 ms (mean: 467 ± 48 ms).
source: Excitatory neurons with pre-I spiking (n = 9; 7 WC, 2 CA) had inspiratory spike frequencies ranging from 12.0 to 50.8 Hz (mean: 28.0 ± 4.4 Hz) and burst durations ranging from 272 to 763 ms (mean: 467 ± 48 ms).
evidence: Experimental data from n=9 neurons

claim: Excitatory neurons without pre-inspiratory spiking (n = 13) had inspiratory spike frequencies ranging from 11.3 to 58.2 Hz (mean: 34.9 ± 4.3 Hz) and burst durations ranging from 242 to 698 ms (mean: 419 ± 34 ms).
source: Similarly, excitatory neurons without pre-I spiking (n = 13; 11 WC, 2 CA) had inspiratory spike frequencies ranging from 11.3 to 58.2 Hz (mean: 34.9 ± 4.3 Hz) and burst durations ranging from 242 to 698 ms (mean: 419 ± 34 ms).
evidence: Experimental data from n=13 neurons

claim: Inhibitory neurons (n = 7) had spike frequencies ranging from 16.4 to 82.9 Hz (mean: 48.6 ± 8.6 Hz) and burst durations ranging from 144 to 517 ms (mean: 316 ± 54 ms).
source: Inhibitory neurons (n = 7; 5 WC, 2 CA) also had considerable variability in spike frequency (16.4 to 82.9 Hz; mean: 48.6 ± 8.6 Hz) and burst duration (144 to 517 ms; mean: 316 ± 54 ms) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Experimental data from n=7 neurons

claim: Inhibitory neurons had a much more pronounced decrementing spiking pattern than excitatory neurons with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 24 ± 7% of the inspiratory burst duration.
source: Inhibitory neurons had a much more pronounced decrementing spiking pattern than excitatory neurons with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 24 ± 7% of the inspiratory burst duration.
evidence: Experimental data from n=7 inhibitory neurons

claim: Excitatory neurons with pre-inspiratory spiking exhibited a rounded burst pattern with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 49 ± 5% of the inspiratory burst duration.
source: Excitatory neurons with pre-I spiking exhibited a rounded burst pattern with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 49 ± 5% of the inspiratory burst duration, whereas excitatory neurons without pre-I spiking were slightly more decrementing with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 34 ± 6% of the inspiratory burst duration.
evidence: Experimental data from n=9 pre-I excitatory neurons

claim: Excitatory neurons without pre-inspiratory spiking were slightly more decrementing with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 34 ± 6% of the inspiratory burst duration.
source: Excitatory neurons with pre-I spiking exhibited a rounded burst pattern with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 49 ± 5% of the inspiratory burst duration, whereas excitatory neurons without pre-I spiking were slightly more decrementing with maximal spike frequencies occurring at 34 ± 6% of the inspiratory burst duration.
evidence: Experimental data from n=13 non pre-I excitatory neurons

claim: Excitatory neurons with pre-inspiratory spiking had more cycle-to-cycle variability in burst onset times than excitatory neurons without pre-inspiratory spiking or inhibitory neurons (p<0.001).
source: Overall, average onset times did not differ among neuron types (p>0.05); however, excitatory neurons with pre-I spiking had more cycle-to-cycle variability in burst onset times than excitatory neurons without pre-I spiking or inhibitory neurons (p<0.001).
evidence: Experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Substance P had little effect on spiking during inspiratory bursts in pre-inspiratory neurons.
source: Unexpectedly, SP had little effect on spiking during inspiratory bursts (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental observation from n=9 pre-I neurons

claim: In pre-inspiratory neurons, changes in burst spike frequency (28.0 ± 4.4 Hz to 29.6 ± 3.8 Hz, p>0.05) and burst duration (467 ± 78 ms to 488 ± 45 ms; p>0.05) induced by substance P were small and inconsistent.
source: Changes in burst spike frequency (28.0 ± 4.4 Hz to 29.6 ± 3.8 Hz, p>0.05) and burst duration (467 ± 78 ms to 488 ± 45 ms; p>0.05) were small and inconsistent (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Experimental data from n=9 pre-I neurons with statistical analysis

claim: During the inter-burst interval, substance P increased the average spiking frequency of pre-inspiratory neurons from 5.1 ± 1.0 Hz to 9.9 ± 1.8 Hz (p<0.01).
source: In contrast, during the IBI, SP increased the average spiking frequency of pre-I neurons from 5.1 ± 1.0 Hz to 9.9 ± 1.8 Hz (p<0.01), and in all cases increased the slope of the pre-inspiratory ramp (average of 1.7 ± 0.8 to 3.7 ± 1.9 Hz/sec), although this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.113) due to the large variability among neurons (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Experimental data from n=9 pre-I neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Substance P increased the slope of the pre-inspiratory ramp in all pre-inspiratory neurons (average of 1.7 ± 0.8 to 3.7 ± 1.9 Hz/sec), although this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.113) due to the large variability among neurons.
source: In contrast, during the IBI, SP increased the average spiking frequency of pre-I neurons from 5.1 ± 1.0 Hz to 9.9 ± 1.8 Hz (p<0.01), and in all cases increased the slope of the pre-inspiratory ramp (average of 1.7 ± 0.8 to 3.7 ± 1.9 Hz/sec), although this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.113) due to the large variability among neurons (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Experimental data from n=9 pre-I neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Under control conditions and in substance P, there was a significant inverse relationship between the duration of a given inter-burst interval and the slope of the corresponding pre-inspiratory ramp.
source: We found that, under control conditions and in SP, there was a significant inverse relationship between the duration of a given IBI and the slope of the corresponding pre-inspiratory ramp, such that pre-inspiratory spiking activity at the level of individual neurons can predict the duration between inspiratory bursts at the network level.
evidence: Experimental data from n=9 neurons (20 consecutive IBIs/neuron) with linear regression analysis

claim: Pre-inspiratory spiking activity at the level of individual neurons can predict the duration between inspiratory bursts at the network level.
source: We found that, under control conditions and in SP, there was a significant inverse relationship between the duration of a given IBI and the slope of the corresponding pre-inspiratory ramp, such that pre-inspiratory spiking activity at the level of individual neurons can predict the duration between inspiratory bursts at the network level.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing inverse relationship between IBI duration and pre-inspiratory ramp slope

claim: In response to substance P, some excitatory neurons that did not spike during the inter-burst interval under baseline conditions (8/13) remained silent during the inter-burst interval, whereas others (5/13) developed pre-inspiratory spiking.
source: In response to SP, excitatory neurons that did not spike during the IBI under baseline conditions exhibited two distinct phenotypes. Some (8/13) remained silent during the IBI (teal), whereas others (5/13) developed pre-inspiratory spiking (green) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental observation from n=13 excitatory neurons without pre-I spiking at baseline

claim: Excitatory neurons that were not recruited to spike during the inter-burst interval by substance P (n = 8) had no change in spike frequency (38.6 ± 5.0 to 37.1 ± 4.9 Hz; p>0.05) or burst duration (430 ± 53 to 428 ± 51 ms, p>0.05) during inspiratory bursts.
source: Excitatory neurons that were not recruited to spike during the IBI (n = 7 WC, 1 CA) also had no change in spike frequency (38.6 ± 5.0 to 37.1 ± 4.9 Hz; p>0.05) or burst duration (430 ± 53 to 428 ± 51 ms, p>0.05) during inspiratory bursts (Figure 4B,C), despite a shortened IBI duration (p<0.05).
evidence: Experimental data from n=8 excitatory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: In excitatory neurons that were recruited to spike during the inter-burst interval by substance P (n = 5), spiking frequency increased from 0 to 6.6 ± 1.4 Hz (p<0.01).
source: In neurons that were recruited to spike during the IBI (n = 4 WC, 1 CA), spiking frequency increased from 0 to 6.6 ± 1.4 Hz (p<0.01).
evidence: Experimental data from n=5 excitatory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: In substance P, excitatory neurons recruited to spike during the inter-burst interval exhibited a pre-inspiratory ramp (4.1 ± 1.7 Hz/sec).
source: In SP, these neurons exhibited a pre-inspiratory ramp (4.1 ± 1.7 Hz/sec), which was coincident with a shorter IBI duration (p<0.05) (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Experimental data from n=5 excitatory neurons

claim: In excitatory neurons recruited to pre-inspiratory activity by substance P, the slope of the SP-induced pre-inspiratory ramp had a significant inverse relationship with the duration of the inter-burst interval during individual inspiratory cycles.
source: During individual inspiratory cycles, the slope of the SP-induced pre-inspiratory ramp had a significant inverse relationship with the duration of the IBI (Figure 4F).
evidence: Experimental data from n=5 neurons (20 consecutive IBIs/neuron) with linear regression analysis

claim: In excitatory neurons recruited to pre-inspiratory activity by substance P, spiking patterns during inspiratory bursts did not change in spike frequency (28.9 ± 7.8 to 31.9 ± 6.6 Hz, p>0.05), burst duration (399 ± 28 to 441 ± 36 ms, p>0.05), or burst shape.
source: During inspiratory bursts, spiking patterns did not change in spike frequency (28.9 ± 7.8 to 31.9 ± 6.6 Hz, p>0.05), burst duration (399 ± 28 to 441 ± 36 ms, p>0.05), or burst shape (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Experimental data from n=5 excitatory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: A subpopulation of non pre-inspiratory excitatory neurons develops pre-inspiratory activity in substance P without a change in spiking activity during bursts.
source: Thus, a subpopulation of non pre-I excitatory neurons develops pre-I activity in SP without a change in spiking activity during bursts, suggesting that the number of neurons that can participate in the percolation phase increases in the presence of SP, without significant effects on the amount of excitation during bursts and the resulting refractory period.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing recruitment to pre-I activity without changes in burst spiking

claim: The number of neurons that can participate in the percolation phase increases in the presence of substance P, without significant effects on the amount of excitation during bursts and the resulting refractory period.
source: Thus, a subpopulation of non pre-I excitatory neurons develops pre-I activity in SP without a change in spiking activity during bursts, suggesting that the number of neurons that can participate in the percolation phase increases in the presence of SP, without significant effects on the amount of excitation during bursts and the resulting refractory period.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing recruitment to pre-I activity without changes in burst spiking

claim: Spike frequency and burst duration of inspiratory inhibitory neurons in the preBötC did not change during bursts in the presence of substance P (48.6 ± 8.6 to 43.5 ± 6.7 Hz, p>0.05; and 316 ± 54 to 328 ± 56 ms, p>0.05, respectively).
source: In the presence of SP, spike frequency and burst duration of inspiratory inhibitory neurons did not change during bursts (48.6 ± 8.6 to 43.5 ± 6.7 Hz, p>0.05; and 316 ± 54 to 328 ± 56 ms, p>0.05, respectively), despite a coincident shortening of the IBI (p<0.05) (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Experimental data from n=7 inhibitory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Spiking activity of inhibitory neurons in the preBötC did not change during the inter-burst interval in response to substance P, since all recorded neurons remained silent between inspiratory bursts.
source: Spiking activity of inhibitory neurons also did not change during the IBI, since all recorded neurons remained silent between inspiratory bursts.
evidence: Experimental observation from n=7 inhibitory neurons

claim: In response to substance P, inhibitory neurons in the preBötC had no change in spiking throughout the inspiratory cycle and are therefore unlikely to play a role in SP-induced facilitation of inspiratory frequency.
source: Thus, in response to SP, inhibitory neurons in the preBötC had no change in spiking throughout the inspiratory cycle and are therefore unlikely to play a role in SP-induced facilitation of inspiratory frequency.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing no change in inhibitory neuron spiking

claim: Substance P increased the stochasticity of burst onset in a subgroup of preBötC excitatory neurons.
source: These results suggest that SP increases the stochasticity of burst onset in a subgroup of preBötC excitatory neurons.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing increased burst onset jitter

claim: Burst onset jitter of excitatory pre-inspiratory neurons did not change significantly in substance P (p>0.05).
source: Burst onset jitter of excitatory pre-I neurons, which was generally high under baseline conditions (see Figure 2F), did not change significantly in SP (p>0.05) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Experimental data from n=9 pre-I neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Excitatory neurons that did not exhibit pre-inspiratory spiking and had relatively low onset jitter under baseline conditions exhibited increased onset jitter in the presence of substance P (p<0.05).
source: In contrast, excitatory neurons that did not exhibit pre-I spiking and had relatively low onset jitter under baseline conditions exhibited increased onset jitter in the presence of SP (p<0.05).
evidence: Experimental data from n=13 non pre-I excitatory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Among excitatory neurons without pre-inspiratory spiking at baseline, burst onset jitter was increased by substance P regardless of whether or not the neuron was recruited to develop pre-inspiratory spiking.
source: Among this group of excitatory neurons, burst onset jitter was increased by SP regardless of whether or not the neuron was recruited to develop pre-inspiratory spiking.
evidence: Experimental observation from n=13 non pre-I excitatory neurons

claim: Inhibitory preBötC neurons had relatively inconsistent changes in burst onset variability induced by substance P, with no change in mean onset jitter (p>0.05).
source: Inhibitory preBötC neurons, on the other hand, had relatively inconsistent changes in burst onset variability induced by SP, with no change in mean onset jitter (p>0.05).
evidence: Experimental data from n=7 inhibitory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: The increase in stochasticity at the level of individual neurons induced by substance P was reflected in the activity of the preBötC network as a slight increase in the duration (707 ± 22 to 854 ± 33 ms; p<0.0001) and halfwidth (429 ± 18 to 478 ± 20 ms; p<0.0001) of population bursts.
source: Indeed, this increase in stochasticity at the level of individual neurons was reflected in the activity of the preBötC network as a slight increase in the duration (707 ± 22 to 854 ± 33 ms; p<0.0001) and halfwidth (429 ± 18 to 478 ± 20 ms; p<0.0001) of population bursts in SP (Figure 6C).
evidence: Experimental data from n=29 slices with statistical analysis

claim: Substance P increases the frequency and stability of the inspiratory rhythm in transverse slices that isolate the preBötC from the rest of the ventral respiratory column.
source: Substance P increase the frequency and stability of the inspiratory rhythm in transverse slices that isolate the preBötC from the rest of the ventral respiratory column (VRC) (Gray et al., 1999; Peña and Ramirez, 2004b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gray et al., 1999; Peña and Ramirez, 2004b

claim: Neurons with inspiratory activity are distributed along the ventral respiratory column.
source: However, neurons with inspiratory activity are not confined to the preBötC but are distributed along the VRC (Barnes et al., 2007; Zuperku et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barnes et al., 2007; Zuperku et al., 2019

claim: Excitatory neurons located rostral to the preBötC can be conditionally recruited to participate in the inspiratory rhythm.
source: Indeed, the inspiratory network seems to be spatially dynamic since excitatory neurons located rostral to the preBötC can be conditionally recruited to participate in the inspiratory rhythm (Baertsch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baertsch et al., 2019

claim: Rostral expansion of the active inspiratory network is associated with an increase in the excitation/inhibition ratio, longer refractory times, and slower inspiratory frequencies.
source: This rostral expansion of the active inspiratory network is associated with an increase in the excitation/inhibition ratio, longer refractory times, and slower inspiratory frequencies (Baertsch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baertsch et al., 2019

claim: Spiking frequency during bursts was reduced by substance P in all (5/5) rostral excitatory neurons (−55.6 ± 13.5% change from 11.1 ± 4.7 to 6.7 ± 4.0 Hz; p<0.05).
source: Despite this variability, spiking frequency during bursts was reduced by SP in all (5/5) rostral excitatory neurons (−55.6 ± 13.5% change from 11.1 ± 4.7 to 6.7 ± 4.0 Hz; p<0.05) (Figure 8A,C), whereas changes were inconsistent among inhibitory rostral neurons with no change on average (39.5 ± 34.7% change from 5.3 ± 1.5 to 6.1 ± 1.5 Hz; p>0.05) (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Experimental data from n=5 rostral excitatory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Changes in spiking frequency during bursts induced by substance P were inconsistent among inhibitory rostral neurons with no change on average (39.5 ± 34.7% change from 5.3 ± 1.5 to 6.1 ± 1.5 Hz; p>0.05).
source: Despite this variability, spiking frequency during bursts was reduced by SP in all (5/5) rostral excitatory neurons (−55.6 ± 13.5% change from 11.1 ± 4.7 to 6.7 ± 4.0 Hz; p<0.05) (Figure 8A,C), whereas changes were inconsistent among inhibitory rostral neurons with no change on average (39.5 ± 34.7% change from 5.3 ± 1.5 to 6.1 ± 1.5 Hz; p>0.05) (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Experimental data from n=7 rostral inhibitory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: The potential contribution of rostral excitatory neurons to synchronization of the inspiratory rhythm was reduced by substance P, while inhibitory influences were relatively unchanged.
source: Thus, the potential contribution of rostral excitatory neurons to synchronization of the inspiratory rhythm was reduced by SP, while inhibitory influences were relatively unchanged.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing reduced excitatory but unchanged inhibitory spiking in rostral neurons

claim: Burst onset variability of both excitatory and inhibitory inspiratory neurons rostral of the preBötC was generally high under baseline conditions, and it was further increased by substance P (p<0.05).
source: Burst onset variability of both excitatory and inhibitory inspiratory neurons rostral of the preBötC was generally high under baseline conditions, and it was further increased by SP (p<0.05) (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: Experimental data from n=5 excitatory and n=7 inhibitory rostral neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Excitatory rostral neurons were generally silent during the inter-burst interval under baseline conditions, and they remained silent following application of substance P.
source: Unlike the pre-I spiking described for excitatory neurons in the preBötC (see Figures 3 and 4), excitatory rostral neurons were generally silent during the IBI under baseline conditions, and they remained silent following application of SP (Figure 7B).
evidence: Experimental observation from n=5 rostral excitatory neurons

claim: Four out of seven inhibitory rostral neurons exhibited spiking during the inter-burst interval under baseline conditions.
source: In contrast, four out of seven inhibitory rostral neurons exhibited spiking during the IBI under baseline conditions, and in three of these neurons spike frequency during the IBI was increased by SP.
evidence: Experimental observation from n=7 rostral inhibitory neurons

claim: In three of the four inhibitory rostral neurons that exhibited spiking during the inter-burst interval under baseline conditions, spike frequency during the inter-burst interval was increased by substance P.
source: In contrast, four out of seven inhibitory rostral neurons exhibited spiking during the IBI under baseline conditions, and in three of these neurons spike frequency during the IBI was increased by SP.
evidence: Experimental observation from n=7 rostral inhibitory neurons

claim: Among the three inhibitory rostral neurons that were silent during the inter-burst interval under baseline conditions, two were recruited to spike during the inter-burst interval in response to substance P.
source: Among the three inhibitory rostral neurons that were silent during the IBI under baseline conditions, two were recruited to spike during the IBI in response to SP.
evidence: Experimental observation from n=7 rostral inhibitory neurons

claim: Overall, six of seven inhibitory rostral neurons exhibited spiking during the inter-burst interval in substance P (1.5 ± 0.6 Hz at baseline to 3.5 ± 1.2 Hz in SP; p>0.05).
source: Overall, six of seven exhibited spiking during the IBI in SP (1.5 ± 0.6 Hz at baseline to 3.5 ± 1.2 Hz in SP; p>0.05) (Figure 8F).
evidence: Experimental data from n=7 rostral inhibitory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: The spiking of inhibitory rostral neurons during the inter-burst interval did not exhibit a pre-inspiratory ramp under baseline conditions (slope: 0.11 ± 0.14 Hz/second; p>0.05) or in the presence of substance P (slope: 0.08 ± 0.15 Hz/second; p>0.05).
source: The spiking of these neurons did not exhibit a pre-inspiratory ramp under baseline conditions (slope: 0.11 ± 0.14 Hz/second; p>0.05) or in the presence of SP (slope: 0.08 ± 0.15 Hz/second; p>0.05), suggesting changes in the spiking of these inhibitory neurons during the IBI is not be regulated by excitatory pre-I neurons in the preBötC.
evidence: Experimental data from n=7 rostral inhibitory neurons with statistical analysis

claim: Changes in the spiking of inhibitory rostral neurons during the inter-burst interval are not regulated by excitatory pre-inspiratory neurons in the preBötC.
source: The spiking of these neurons did not exhibit a pre-inspiratory ramp under baseline conditions (slope: 0.11 ± 0.14 Hz/second; p>0.05) or in the presence of SP (slope: 0.08 ± 0.15 Hz/second; p>0.05), suggesting changes in the spiking of these inhibitory neurons during the IBI is not be regulated by excitatory pre-I neurons in the preBötC.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing no pre-inspiratory ramp in rostral inhibitory neurons

claim: Changes in neuromodulatory systems within the brainstem have been linked to many respiratory control disorders.
source: Changes in neuromodulatory systems within the brainstem have been linked to many of these and other respiratory control disorders (Doi and Ramirez, 2008; Viemari et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doi and Ramirez, 2008; Viemari et al., 2005

claim: Distinct phases of the rhythmogenic process can be differentially regulated by neuromodulation to dynamically control the frequency and stability of breathing.
source: Here, we introduce the concept that distinct phases of the rhythmogenic process can be differentially regulated by neuromodulation to dynamically control the frequency and stability of breathing (Figure 9).
evidence: Conceptual framework proposed based on experimental findings

claim: During inspiration, each burst is assembled stochastically via heterogeneous interactions among a combination of intertwined synaptic and intrinsic properties.
source: During inspiration, each burst is assembled stochastically via heterogeneous interactions among a combination of intertwined synaptic and intrinsic properties (Ramirez and Baertsch, 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramirez and Baertsch, 2018b

claim: The combination of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic interactions with intrinsic bursting properties, known as the 'rhythmogenic triangle', is critical for the flexibility of the inspiratory network.
source: To the contrary, the combination of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic interactions with intrinsic bursting properties, known as the 'rhythmogenic triangle' (Ramirez and Baertsch, 2018b), is critical for the flexibility of this dynamic network (Ramirez et al., 2004; Rubin and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2000; Richter and Smith, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ramirez and Baertsch, 2018b; Ramirez et al., 2004; Rubin and Smith, 2019; Smith et al., 2000; Richter and Smith, 2014

claim: In invertebrate model systems, neuromodulators can inhibit or strengthen synaptic interactions.
source: In these networks, neuromodulators can inhibit or strengthen synaptic interactions (Harris-Warrick et al., 1998; Marder et al., 2014; Nusbaum et al., 2001), as well as induce or suppress intrinsic bursting properties (Elson and Selverston, 1992; Flamm and Harris-Warrick, 1986; Zhang and Harris-Warrick, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris-Warrick et al., 1998; Marder et al., 2014; Nusbaum et al., 2001

claim: In invertebrate model systems, neuromodulators can induce or suppress intrinsic bursting properties.
source: In these networks, neuromodulators can inhibit or strengthen synaptic interactions (Harris-Warrick et al., 1998; Marder et al., 2014; Nusbaum et al., 2001), as well as induce or suppress intrinsic bursting properties (Elson and Selverston, 1992; Flamm and Harris-Warrick, 1986; Zhang and Harris-Warrick, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Elson and Selverston, 1992; Flamm and Harris-Warrick, 1986; Zhang and Harris-Warrick, 1994

claim: Principles of neuromodulation observed in invertebrate networks also apply to the aminergic and peptidergic modulation of the mammalian preBötC network.
source: These important principles also apply to the aminergic and peptidergic modulation of the mammalian preBötC network (Doi and Ramirez, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doi and Ramirez, 2010

claim: In the absence of synaptic interactions, the activity of both INaP and ICAN-dependent autonomous bursting neurons in the preBötC is modulated by substance P.
source: For example, in the absence of synaptic interactions, the activity of both INaP and ICAN-dependent autonomous bursting neurons in the preBötC is modulated by SP (Ben-Mabrouk and Tryba, 2010; Peña and Ramirez, 2004b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ben-Mabrouk and Tryba, 2010; Peña and Ramirez, 2004b

claim: NK1R expressing preBötC neurons are important for rhythmogenesis.
source: Although it is known that NK1R expressing preBötC neurons are important for rhythmogenesis (Gray et al., 2001; Guyenet and Wang, 2001), it is unclear how these modulatory effects regulate the frequency and stability of the inspiratory rhythm.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gray et al., 2001; Guyenet and Wang, 2001

claim: NK1R is primarily expressed on excitatory neurons in the preBötC.
source: Evidence suggests that NK1R is primarily expressed on excitatory neurons (Gray et al., 1999), including those with pre-I activity (Guyenet and Wang, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gray et al., 1999; Guyenet and Wang, 2001

claim: NK1R is expressed on excitatory neurons with pre-inspiratory activity.
source: Evidence suggests that NK1R is primarily expressed on excitatory neurons (Gray et al., 1999), including those with pre-I activity (Guyenet and Wang, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guyenet and Wang, 2001

claim: Substance P does not affect the spiking frequency of either excitatory or inhibitory preBötC neurons during the inspiratory burst phase.
source: Instead, we found that SP does not affect the spiking frequency of either excitatory or inhibitory preBötC neurons during the inspiratory burst phase (Figures 3, 4 and 5).
evidence: Experimental data from Figures 3, 4, and 5

claim: The balance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs to preBötC neurons is not changed by substance P.
source: Accordingly, we suggest that the balance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs to preBötC neurons is not changed by SP, although voltage-clamp experiments under visual control would be warranted to more directly assess this balance.
evidence: Inference from current clamp recordings showing no change in spiking during bursts

claim: Transverse brainstem slice preparations that lack rostral inspiratory neurons generate less robust rhythms with shorter refractory periods and faster frequencies than horizontal slices.
source: Indeed, transverse brainstem slice preparations that lack rostral inspiratory neurons generate less robust rhythms with shorter refractory periods and faster frequencies than horizontal slices (Baertsch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baertsch et al., 2019

claim: Recruitment of rostral inspiratory neurons is associated with increased excitation during inspiratory bursts, a prolonged refractory phase, and consequently slower breathing frequencies.
source: On the other hand, recruitment of these neurons is associated with increased excitation during inspiratory bursts, a prolonged refractory phase, and consequently slower breathing frequencies (Baertsch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baertsch et al., 2019

claim: Under normal conditions, inhibition restrains the rhythm generating ability of rostral inspiratory neurons allowing faster, more dynamic breathing.
source: However, under normal conditions, inhibition restrains the rhythm generating ability of these rostral neurons allowing faster, more dynamic breathing.
evidence: Inference from established knowledge about rostral neuron regulation

claim: The contribution of rostral inspiratory neurons to SP-induced frequency increase seems to be relatively modest.
source: Thus, unlike their role in modulating other dynamic breathing responses such as gasping (Baertsch et al., 2019), the contribution of rostral inspiratory neurons to SP-induced frequency increase seems to be relatively modest.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing heterogeneous effects of SP on rostral neurons

claim: NK1R is preferentially expressed in the preBötC compared to other regions of the ventral respiratory column.
source: Indeed, NK1R is preferentially expressed in the preBötC compared to other regions of the ventral respiratory column (Gray et al., 1999), which may explain the relatively heterogeneous effects of SP on the activity of rostral neurons (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gray et al., 1999

claim: The assembly of inspiratory bursts is stochastic, which is observed as significant variability in the cycle-to-cycle onset time of inspiratory neuron bursts relative to the preBötC population.
source: The assembly of inspiratory bursts is known to be stochastic, which is observed as significant variability in the cycle-to-cycle onset time of inspiratory neuron bursts relative to the preBötC population (Carroll and Ramirez, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carroll and Ramirez, 2013

claim: Variability in activation order, or onset jitter, is related, at least in part, to the sparse functional connectivity within the preBötC network.
source: This variability in activation order, or onset jitter, is related, at least in part, to the sparse functional connectivity within the preBötC network (Carroll and Ramirez, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carroll and Ramirez, 2013

claim: Substance P increases the variability of burst onset times among inspiratory neurons located within and rostral to the preBötC.
source: We found that SP increases the variability of burst onset times among inspiratory neurons located within and rostral to the preBötC.
evidence: Experimental data from n=29 neurons

claim: The increase in timing variability induced by substance P was most pronounced among excitatory neurons, specifically those that lack pre-inspiratory activity.
source: This increase in timing variability was most pronounced among excitatory neurons, specifically those that lack pre-I activity (Figure 6).
evidence: Experimental data from Figure 6

claim: Increased jitter among excitatory neurons impairs synchronization of the network and helps maintain the balance of excitation and inhibition during inspiratory bursts in the presence of substance P.
source: Thus, although other mechanisms such as depletion of excitatory synaptic vesicles (Rubin et al., 2009) may also contribute, we propose that increased jitter among excitatory neurons impairs synchronization of the network and helps maintain the balance of excitation and inhibition during inspiratory bursts in the presence of SP.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental data and inference

claim: The inspiratory burst phase is followed by a period of reduced excitability in the preBötC network called the refractory period.
source: The inspiratory burst phase is followed by a period of reduced excitability in the preBötC network.
evidence: Experimental observation from optogenetic stimulation experiments

claim: The refractory period is thought to arise from a combination of presynaptic depression and activation of slow hyperpolarizing current(s) in glutamatergic Dbx1 neurons during inspiratory bursts.
source: This refractory period is thought to arise from a combination of presynaptic depression (Kottick and Del Negro, 2015) and activation of slow hyperpolarizing current(s) (Baertsch et al., 2018; Krey et al., 2010) in glutamatergic Dbx1 neurons during inspiratory bursts.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kottick and Del Negro, 2015; Baertsch et al., 2018; Krey et al., 2010

claim: Refractoriness is maximal immediately following the inspiratory burst followed by a gradual recovery of excitability.
source: Indeed, refractoriness is maximal immediately following the inspiratory burst followed by a gradual recovery of excitability (Figure 1), likely as vesicles are recycled and hyperpolarizing conductances are inactivated.
evidence: Experimental data from Figure 1 and inference about underlying mechanisms

claim: The refractory period manifests experimentally as a period during which the probability of evoking an ectopic inspiratory burst via optogenetic stimulation of Dbx1 neurons is reduced.
source: This refractory phase manifests experimentally as a period during which the probability of evoking an ectopic inspiratory burst via optogenetic stimulation of Dbx1 neurons is reduced (Figure 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from Figure 1A

claim: The refractory period is not absolute as it can be overcome if the stimulus is of sufficient strength.
source: However, the refractory period is not absolute as it can be overcome if the stimulus is of sufficient strength (Vann et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vann et al., 2018

claim: The minimum duration of spontaneous inter-burst intervals continues to be restrained by the refractory period in substance P.
source: Importantly, the minimum duration of spontaneous inter-burst intervals continues to be restrained by the refractory period in SP (Figure 1).
evidence: Experimental data from Figure 1

claim: Refractory mechanisms remain an important determinant of breathing frequency in the presence of substance P.
source: Thus, refractory mechanisms remain an important determinant of breathing frequency in the presence of this neuromodulator.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing refractory period constrains IBIs in SP

claim: Refractory mechanisms may be functionally important to prevent excitatory neuromodulators such as substance P from driving the respiratory network out of its physiological frequency range.
source: This may be functionally important to prevent excitatory neuromodulators such as SP from driving the respiratory network out of its physiological frequency range.
evidence: Speculation about functional significance based on experimental findings

claim: Neuronal networks must be capable of dynamically regulating their frequency while maintaining stability in spite of heterogeneous, intrinsically variable cellular components that receive converging inputs from numerous excitatory neuromodulators.
source: Indeed, neuronal networks must not only be capable of dynamically regulating their frequency, but they must also be able to maintain stability in spite of heterogeneous, intrinsically variable cellular components that receive converging inputs from numerous excitatory neuromodulators (Marder et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marder et al., 2014

claim: As the inspiratory network transitions out of the refractory phase, some excitatory neurons begin to fire action potentials prior to the onset of the next synchronized population burst.
source: As the inspiratory network transitions out of the refractory phase, some excitatory neurons, presumably with more depolarized basal membrane potentials (Butera et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000), begin to fire action potentials prior to the onset of the next synchronized population burst (Figure 3).
evidence: Experimental data from Figure 3 and supported by citations to Butera et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2000

claim: The associated synaptic interactions during the percolation phase may particularly involve Dbx1 neurons.
source: The associated synaptic interactions, which may particularly involve Dbx1 neurons (Wang et al., 2014), are thought to stochastically percolate through a network of recurrently connected excitatory neurons (Del Negro et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2014; Del Negro et al., 2018

claim: The network-based process of percolation likely occurs simultaneously with changes in intrinsic membrane properties such as INaP.
source: This network-based process, sometimes referred to as the 'group pacemaker' hypothesis (Del Negro and Hayes, 2008), likely occurs simultaneously with changes in intrinsic membrane properties such as INaP (Butera et al., 1999; Ramirez et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2000), that together lead to a gradual build-up of excitability within the network.
evidence: Supported by citations to Del Negro and Hayes, 2008; Butera et al., 1999; Ramirez et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2000

claim: The magnitude and slope of the pre-inspiratory ramp, as well as the number of excitatory neurons that have pre-inspiratory activity, is increased by substance P.
source: We found that the magnitude and slope of this pre-inspiratory ramp, as well as the number of excitatory neurons that have pre-inspiratory activity, is increased by SP.
evidence: Experimental data from Figures 3 and 4

claim: Excitatory neurons recruited to pre-inspiratory activity by substance P exhibit a pronounced pre-inspiratory ramp, suggesting that they participate in the recurrent excitation process.
source: These recruited excitatory neurons also exhibit a pronounced pre-inspiratory ramp, suggesting that they participate in the recurrent excitation process.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing pre-I ramp in recruited neurons

claim: The effects of substance P on pre-inspiratory ramp activity likely increase the rate of recurrent excitation during the percolation phase to accelerate the onset of the next burst.
source: Together, these effects likely increase the rate of recurrent excitation during this percolation phase to accelerate the onset of the next burst (Figure 9), underling the increase in breathing frequency induced by SP.
evidence: Inference from experimental data on pre-I ramp changes

claim: On a cycle-to-cycle basis, the slope of pre-inspiratory ramp activity is inversely related to the inter-burst interval.
source: Moreover, we found that, on a cycle-to-cycle basis, the slope of pre-inspiratory ramp activity is inversely related to the inter-burst interval.
evidence: Experimental data from Figures 3G and 4F with linear regression analysis

claim: Variations in the stochastic percolation of excitation during the percolation phase predict variability in the duration between inspiratory bursts.
source: Thus, variations in the stochastic percolation of excitation during this phase seem to predict variability in the duration between inspiratory bursts.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing relationship between pre-I ramp slope and IBI duration

claim: By increasing the rate of recurrent excitation, substance P makes the percolation process more consistent and breathing irregularity is reduced.
source: Our data suggest that, by increasing the rate of recurrent excitation, this process becomes more consistent and breathing irregularity is reduced.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing increased pre-I ramp slope and reduced IBI variability

claim: The dual effects of substance P on breathing frequency and stability are primarily a consequence of its effects on the percolation phase of the inspiratory rhythm.
source: We conclude that the dual effects of SP on breathing frequency and stability are primarily a consequence of its effects on the percolation phase of the inspiratory rhythm.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental findings

claim: Three distinct phases of the inspiratory rhythm - the burst phase, refractory phase, and percolation phase - can be differentially modulated to influence breathing dynamics and stability.
source: Based on our collective results, we propose a conceptual framework for inspiratory rhythm generation in which three distinct phases, the burst phase, refractory phase, and percolation phase, can be differentially modulated to influence breathing dynamics and stability (Figure 9).
evidence: Conceptual framework proposed based on experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 9

claim: The three phases (burst, refractory, and percolation) are intrinsic to the inspiratory rhythm generator.
source: Although these three phases seem to be intrinsic to the inspiratory rhythm generator, we anticipate that non-inspiratory neurons and/or respiratory related brain regions outside the preBötC (e.g. Anderson et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2019; Huckstepp et al., 2018; Richter and Smith, 2014) can provide important regulatory control over each phase of the inspiratory cycle, leading to predictable phase-dependent effects on rhythm dynamics.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings

claim: Non-inspiratory neurons and/or respiratory related brain regions outside the preBötC can provide important regulatory control over each phase of the inspiratory cycle, leading to predictable phase-dependent effects on rhythm dynamics.
source: Although these three phases seem to be intrinsic to the inspiratory rhythm generator, we anticipate that non-inspiratory neurons and/or respiratory related brain regions outside the preBötC (e.g. Anderson et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2019; Huckstepp et al., 2018; Richter and Smith, 2014) can provide important regulatory control over each phase of the inspiratory cycle, leading to predictable phase-dependent effects on rhythm dynamics.
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2019; Huckstepp et al., 2018; Richter and Smith, 2014

claim: The conceptual framework of three distinct phases may provide a foundation for understanding breathing in the context of many other physiological and pathological conditions.
source: This concept may provide a foundation for understanding breathing in the context of many other physiological and pathological conditions (Bright et al., 2018; Saito et al., 2001), and it may also serve as a guide for understanding the dynamic control rhythm generating networks in general.
evidence: Speculation about broader implications supported by citations to Bright et al., 2018; Saito et al., 2001

claim: The conceptual framework may serve as a guide for understanding the dynamic control of rhythm generating networks in general.
source: This concept may provide a foundation for understanding breathing in the context of many other physiological and pathological conditions (Bright et al., 2018; Saito et al., 2001), and it may also serve as a guide for understanding the dynamic control rhythm generating networks in general.
evidence: Speculation about broader implications
